use_if: Your feature is latency-bound (chat loops, tool-calling agents, real-time UX) and you need sub-200 ms TTFT on open models at zero cost during development. vs OpenRouter: Groq's custom LPU hardware is faster for the models it supports, but you're limited to its model list; OpenRouter gives breadth. vs Cerebras: similar speed story — Groq has a more generous free tier and broader SDK support today.
You need the fastest token generation and your use case fits within daily free limits.

skip_if.reason: Both are speed-focused. Groq has more model variety; Cerebras is similarly fast but with fewer models.

tools.tagline: Very fast inference — good for chat/tool loops before you need GPT-class quality.
tools.about:
Very fast inference — good for chat/tool loops before you need GPT-class quality.

Fastest inference available — LPU hardware delivers tokens at 500+ tok/sec for Llama 70B. Free tier has daily token/request caps but is extremely fast. Ideal for real-time chat and tool-calling loops.

tools.name: Hugging Face Inference
use_if: You want access to the largest catalog of open models (100 K+) with a unified Inference API and free CPU-tier access for experimentation — deploy any model from the Hub without managing infrastructure. vs Together AI / Fireworks: HF Inference has the broadest model selection (including niche fine-tunes); Together/Fireworks are faster and cheaper for the popular models they curate. vs Replicate: HF is better for text/embedding models from the Hub; Replicate's strength is media models (image, video, audio) with per-second billing.
tools.tagline: Hosted open models + embeddings without owning a GPU box.
tools.about: Hosted open models + embeddings without owning a GPU box.

tools.name: Mistral AI API
tools.metric_note: Experiment tier ~1B tokens a month free
limits: Experiment tier ~1B tokens a month free
use_if: You want a European AI provider with a massive free Experiment tier (~1 B tokens/month), strong coding models (Codestral), and both open-weight and proprietary options — good for EU data residency requirements. vs Groq: Mistral's free tier has far higher token limits; Groq is faster but with stricter rate limits. Mistral also offers its own proprietary models (Large, Medium) not available elsewhere. vs OpenAI API: Mistral is significantly cheaper (PAYG from $0.10/MTok vs $2.50+) with competitive quality on many tasks; OpenAI wins on frontier reasoning benchmarks.
You want a strong small model (Nemo 12B) with good instruction following and structured output.

skip_if.reason: Smaller models, more predictable outputs for structured tasks; Gemini is more capable but heavier.

tools.tagline: Strong open-weight and proprietary models — generous free Experiment tier.
tools.about:
Strong open-weight and proprietary models — generous free Experiment tier.

European AI lab's API. Mistral Nemo (12B) is free-tier eligible and good for structured output and function calling. Mistral models tend to be efficient for their size class.

tools.name: Modal
use_if: You need serverless GPU compute for batch jobs — embedding millions of documents, running fine-tunes, or executing custom model code that doesn't fit a managed inference API. vs Replicate: Modal gives you full code control (bring your own Dockerfile, Python, model weights); Replicate is "pick a model from the menu and call it." vs Unsloth on Colab: Modal scales to real batch sizes with persistent storage and cron scheduling; Colab is a free notebook that disconnects after idle.
tools.tagline: Serverless GPU/CPU jobs — batch embeddings and fine-tunes without a cluster.
tools.about: Serverless GPU/CPU jobs — batch embeddings and fine-tunes without a cluster.

tools.name: NVIDIA NIM
use_if: You want to prototype with 100+ models (Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Nemotron) for free via an OpenAI-compatible API — 5,000 credits on signup, no credit card, useful for quick benchmarking across models. vs OpenRouter: NIM is free for prototyping with generous credits; OpenRouter is pay-per-token but production-grade with better routing and fallback. vs Together AI: NIM is for free experimentation (40 RPM cap, not production); Together is PAYG with production SLAs and fine-tuning support.
tools.tagline: 100+ frontier models free via NVIDIA Developer — OpenAI-compatible, no card.
tools.about: 100+ frontier models free via NVIDIA Developer — OpenAI-compatible, no card.

tools.name: OpenAI API
use_if: You need frontier-quality reasoning (GPT-4o, o1) as a fallback when open models or Gemini can't cut it — use project-level spend caps to prevent bill shock and route here only for the hard 10 % of prompts. vs Anthropic API: OpenAI has wider model range (vision, TTS, DALL·E, embeddings in one account); Anthropic is stronger for agentic multi-step tool use and long-form reasoning. vs Google AI Studio: OpenAI has no free tier but often higher benchmark scores on coding and structured output; Gemini wins on cost and context length.
tools.tagline: Pay only when cheaper models fail — wire hard budget alerts day one.
tools.about: Pay only when cheaper models fail — wire hard budget alerts day one.

tools.name: OpenRouter
use_if: You need one API key to access OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, and dozens of open models — swap providers without changing code and use free-tier models for dev. vs Together AI: OpenRouter aggregates *all* providers (closed + open) behind one endpoint; Together only hosts open-weight models. vs direct OpenAI/Anthropic: you trade ~5 % markup for instant fallback routing and cost-ranked model selection.
You want one API key to access many providers and use `:free` models for development/side projects.

skip_if.reason: OpenRouter is a router (many providers); Groq is a single ultra-fast inference provider. OpenRouter's free models rotate; Groq's free tier is more predictable.

tools.tagline: One API for many models — route cheap for drafts, frontier for hard steps.
tools.about:
One API for many models — route cheap for drafts, frontier for hard steps.

Meta-router across 200+ models from dozens of providers. Free-tagged models run at $0 with rate limits. Pay-per-token for everything else. One API key works across all providers, making it ideal as a failover entry point.

tools.name: Replicate
use_if: You need non-text models (image generation, voice cloning, video, upscaling) from a marketplace of community-published models with per-second billing and zero infra management. vs Modal: Replicate is a curated model marketplace you call via API; Modal gives you raw GPU compute to run *your own* code and custom models. vs Stability AI: Replicate hosts Stable Diffusion *plus* thousands of other models (ControlNet, Whisper, RIFE); Stability's API is first-party SD only.
tools.tagline: Run public models (vision, voice, image) without owning GPUs.
tools.about: Run public models (vision, voice, image) without owning GPUs.

tools.name: Stability AI
use_if: You need image generation via API (product shots, illustrations, variations) and want both a managed API with signup credits *and* the option to self-host the same open weights for free on your own GPU. vs Replicate: Stability's API is first-party with latest SD models immediately; Replicate hosts community forks that may lag or diverge. vs DALL·E (OpenAI): Stability is cheaper per image, open-weight (self-host escape hatch), and offers more control (ControlNet, inpainting, upscaling); DALL·E is simpler and better at prompt adherence for non-technical users.
tools.tagline: Stable Diffusion API for image gen — signup credits to start.
tools.about: Stable Diffusion API for image gen — signup credits to start.

tools.name: Together AI
use_if: You want to run Llama, Mixtral, or other open-weight models via API today with an escape hatch to self-host the same weights on your own GPUs later — no vendor lock-in on the model itself. vs Fireworks AI: Together has a wider open-model catalog and fine-tuning support; Fireworks optimizes harder for raw latency on fewer models. vs OpenRouter: Together gives you direct open-weight hosting with fine-tune capability; OpenRouter is an aggregator that can't fine-tune or guarantee which backend serves you.
tools.tagline: Open-weight hosting when you want control without self-hosting GPUs.
tools.about: Open-weight hosting when you want control without self-hosting GPUs.

tools.name: Cohere
use_if: Your RAG pipeline's retrieval quality is the bottleneck and you want best-in-class embeddings plus a reranker endpoint that dramatically improves top-K precision without changing your vector DB. vs Voyage AI: Cohere bundles embeddings *and* rerank in one platform; Voyage has stronger embedding benchmarks but no reranker. vs OpenAI embeddings: Cohere's embed-v3 models are multilingual and retrieval-optimized by design; OpenAI's ada-002 is general-purpose and often weaker for search tasks.
tools.tagline: Embeddings + rerank that often beat generic LLM embeds for retrieval.
tools.about: Embeddings + rerank that often beat generic LLM embeds for retrieval.

tools.name: Together Embeddings
use_if: You want good embeddings at low cost with the guarantee that you can download the same open weights and self-host later — no vendor lock-in on your vector pipeline. vs Voyage AI: Together embeddings are cheaper and open-weight (self-host escape hatch); Voyage has higher retrieval quality on benchmarks but is proprietary and pricier. vs OpenAI ada-002: Together's open models (e.g., BGE, E5) often match or beat ada-002 on retrieval tasks at lower per-token cost, and you own the weights.
You want OpenAI-compatible embeddings from open-weight models with an escape hatch to self-host.

skip_if.reason: Lower quality ceiling but open models mean you can self-host; Voyage is proprietary but higher quality.

tools.tagline: Open-weight embeddings via Together — cheaper RAG than closed APIs.
tools.about:
Open-weight embeddings via Together — cheaper RAG than closed APIs.

Open-weight embedding models hosted. Because the models are open (BGE, E5), you can self-host later without vendor lock-in. OpenAI SDK compatible.

tools.name: Voyage AI
use_if: Retrieval precision is your primary bottleneck and you want embeddings that consistently top MTEB benchmarks for search — Voyage models are purpose-built for retrieval, not general-purpose. vs Cohere: Voyage often leads on raw embedding quality benchmarks; Cohere bundles a reranker you'd need to add separately with Voyage. vs Together Embeddings: Voyage is a specialized embeddings company with top-tier quality; Together offers open-weight embeddings that are cheaper and let you self-host the same model later.
You need the highest-quality embeddings for retrieval/RAG and can afford PAYG after free credits.

skip_if.reason: Better quality for code and retrieval; Together is cheaper at scale with open-weight models.

tools.tagline: Strong embeddings API when retrieval quality matters more than chat.
tools.about:
Strong embeddings API when retrieval quality matters more than chat.

Top-tier embedding quality, especially for code (voyage-code-3) and retrieval tasks. Benchmarks consistently near the top on MTEB. Free credits on signup let you prototype RAG pipelines.

tools.name: Cloudflare Workers AI (Embeddings)
tools.metric_note: Shared 10k neurons a day (with inference budget)
limits: Shared 10k neurons a day (with inference budget)
use_if: Your RAG stack is on Cloudflare (Workers + Vectorize + AI) and you want zero-hop embeddings.

skip_if.reason: Lower quality models (BGE vs Voyage) but free and integrated into Cloudflare; Voyage is better quality but separate infra.

tools.tagline: Embedding generation at the Cloudflare edge.
tools.about: Embedding generation at the Cloudflare edge. Pairs naturally with Vectorize (their vector DB) and Workers for end-to-end RAG without leaving the Cloudflare ecosystem.

tools.name: CodeChum
catches: A discount, not a free tier
use_if: Your CS classes already use it (you probably don't have a choice) — but also if you teach or TA and need a Filipino-context auto-grader that your students already know. It's the de-facto PH college coding platform.

skip_if.reason: HackerRank/LeetCode: CodeChum is institutionally integrated — profs assign via it and grades flow through it. HackerRank is for interview prep; CodeChum is for classroom survival.

tools.tagline: PH auto-grader ubiquitous in college CS — know it even if you don't love it.
tools.about: PH auto-grader ubiquitous in college CS — know it even if you don't love it.

tools.name: Elbi GradeSim
use_if: You're obsessing over whether dropping that 2.5 will cost you Cum Laude, or planning which electives to retake. It simulates GWA scenarios instantly without manual spreadsheet math.

skip_if.reason: manual Excel GWA calculator: GradeSim pulls your actual AMIS grades automatically — no transcription errors, no forgetting that one PE class. Excel is flexible but tedious; GradeSim is instant.

tools.tagline: AMIS grade overlay for GWA / Latin honors simulation — data stays local.
tools.about: AMIS grade overlay for GWA / Latin honors simulation — data stays local.

tools.name: Room TBA
use_if: You regularly need to find which building a class is in, check jeepney schedules, or plan routes — especially when campus Wi-Fi is spotty. The PWA works offline, which is the killer feature.

skip_if.reason: Google Maps: Room TBA knows UPLB building codes and room numbers; Google Maps doesn't. It also integrates class schedules, so you get "where do I go next" not just "navigate to CAS."

tools.tagline: Find UPLB rooms, schedules, jeepney routes — offline-capable PWA.
tools.about: Find UPLB rooms, schedules, jeepney routes — offline-capable PWA.

tools.name: University Edu Email
use_if: You haven't yet activated your university email's hidden perks — GitHub Pro, Azure $100/yr, JetBrains IDEs, Figma Education, and 1TB OneDrive are all gated behind it. Do this on day one of enrollment.

skip_if.reason: personal Gmail for signups: Your .edu email auto-qualifies you for student tiers that personal emails can't access. Some (GitHub Student Pack, Azure) verify via .edu domain alone — no paperwork.

tools.tagline: Your .edu / institutional email unlocks student packs, cloud credits, and pro tools.
tools.about: Your .edu / institutional email unlocks student packs, cloud credits, and pro tools.

tools.name: uplb.tools
use_if: You're a UPLB student and want one bookmark for rooms, grades, and housing instead of juggling SAIS, Facebook groups, and outdated PDFs. It's the unofficial campus Swiss-army knife.

skip_if.reason: official UP SAIS: uplb.tools is faster, mobile-friendly, and adds features SAIS doesn't (grade simulation, route maps). SAIS is authoritative for enrollment; uplb.tools is authoritative for everything else.

tools.tagline: UPLB campus utilities — rooms, gradesim, housing links.
tools.about: UPLB campus utilities — rooms, gradesim, housing links. Privacy-first.

tools.name: 1Password (Pack)
use_if: You juggle dozens of accounts (school, GitHub, cloud consoles, APIs) and want a password manager that also handles SSH keys, CLI secrets, and `.env` injection via Developer Tools — solving both security hygiene and dev workflow in one app.
tools.tagline: Password manager + Developer Tools for a year.
tools.about:
Password manager + Developer Tools for a year.

vs Bitwarden (free forever) / KeePass: Bitwarden is free indefinitely and open-source, but lacks native SSH agent integration and `.env` injection. KeePass is offline-only and clunky on mobile. 1Password wins on developer UX — but export your vault before the year ends and decide if the paid price is worth it post-student.

tools.name: Adobe Creative Cloud Student
catches: A discount, not a free tier
use_if: Your workflow demands Photoshop, Premiere, or After Effects specifically — because your team shares .psd/.aep files, or an internship requires Adobe deliverables. The discount makes the ~$23/mo sting less, but it still stings.

skip_if.reason: Figma + DaVinci Resolve: For UI design + video editing alone, Figma (free) plus DaVinci Resolve (free) covers 80% of use cases at $0. Adobe only wins when you need the exact Adobe file format or a tool like Illustrator's print-press output.

tools.tagline: All Apps cheaper — still a subscription.
tools.about: All Apps cheaper — still a subscription.

tools.name: Autodesk Education
use_if: Your coursework requires parametric CAD (mechanical parts in Fusion 360), architectural BIM (Revit), or film-grade 3D animation (Maya). These are industry-standard desktop apps with no browser equivalent.

skip_if.reason: Blender: Blender covers organic modeling and animation for free, but lacks parametric CAD constraints and BIM workflows. If your professor specifies Revit drawings or STEP exports, Autodesk is the only free path.

tools.tagline: AutoCAD, Fusion 360, Maya, Revit — renewable yearly.
tools.about: AutoCAD, Fusion 360, Maya, Revit — renewable yearly.

tools.name: Azure for Students Starter
use_if: You're under 18 or can't get the full Azure for Students $100 credit — this no-credit-card tier gives you App Service, Functions, and Cognitive Services with caps, enough to deploy a web app or API for a class project without any billing risk.
tools.tagline: No-card starter cloud for younger students — App Service / Functions caps.
tools.about:
No-card starter cloud for younger students — App Service / Functions caps.

vs Azure for Students ($100 credit): The full Azure for Students is strictly better if you qualify — more services, VMs, and flexibility. Use Starter only if age or verification blocks the main offer. Don't use both simultaneously; they're separate programs with separate limits.

tools.name: Azure for Students
catches: Credit runs out if you leave VMs on
use_if: You need real cloud VMs, databases, or Azure-specific services (Cosmos DB, Functions, AKS) for coursework or personal projects and want to learn enterprise cloud without bill anxiety. The no-credit-card requirement means zero risk of surprise charges.
tools.tagline: $100 credit/year, no credit card, renewable while enrolled.
tools.about:
$100 credit/year, no credit card, renewable while enrolled.

vs AWS Free Tier / GCP Credits: AWS free tier is perpetual but thin (t2.micro only), and requires a credit card. GCP student credits exist but are harder to find and one-shot. Azure renews annually with no card — the safest "learn cloud" sandbox for students who forget to tear down resources.

tools.name: Canva Education
use_if: You need quick social media graphics, slide decks, or print posters without learning Figma or Illustrator. The drag-and-drop template library is unmatched for non-designers who still want polished output.

skip_if.reason: Figma is a precision UI/UX tool for developers and designers building interfaces. Canva is a marketing/content tool for fast visual assets. If you're designing app screens, use Figma; if you're making an event flyer in 10 minutes, use Canva.

tools.tagline: Canva Pro features free for verified students and teachers.
tools.about: Canva Pro features free for verified students and teachers.

tools.name: Datadog (Pack)
use_if: You run services (homelab, side projects, cloud VMs) and want real APM, log aggregation, and dashboards to understand what's happening in production — the kind of observability stack companies pay $20k+/yr for, handed to you free for learning.
tools.tagline: Pro monitoring via GitHub Student Pack — don't leave it unclaimed.
tools.about:
Pro monitoring via GitHub Student Pack — don't leave it unclaimed.

vs Grafana Cloud Free / Uptime Kuma: Grafana Cloud free gives you metrics + logs but limited retention and no APM traces. Uptime Kuma is self-hosted ping monitoring only. Datadog Pro gives you full distributed tracing, error tracking, and infra maps — overkill for a single container, perfect for learning enterprise observability patterns.

tools.name: Figma Education
use_if: You need unlimited projects, shared team libraries, and branching — the full Professional feature set — without paying $15/seat/mo. You're enrolled in higher-ed and can re-verify yearly.

skip_if.reason: Starter caps you at 3 Figma files and 3 FigJam files per team; Education unlocks unlimited files, shared libraries, and dev-mode — the tools you actually need for group capstone work.

tools.tagline: Professional plan free for higher-ed students.
tools.about: Professional plan free for higher-ed students.

tools.name: GitHub Codespaces
use_if: Your local machine is underpowered, shared, or locked-down — Codespaces gives you a full Linux dev box in seconds from any browser or thin client. Also ideal when you switch between machines (library desktop → laptop → tablet) and want identical environments without dotfile gymnastics.
tools.tagline: Cloud dev environments on your personal account.
tools.about:
Cloud dev environments on your personal account.

vs Gitpod / local Docker: Gitpod's free tier is stingier on hours and lacks the native GitHub integration (PR codespaces, deep linking). Local Docker is free but requires a capable machine and setup time. Codespaces trades hours-per-month for zero-config parity across devices.

tools.name: GitHub Copilot Student
use_if: You're writing code daily and want inline completions that cut boilerplate in half — especially repetitive tests, data transformations, and API glue. The student tier is the same Pro product; no feature gates.
tools.tagline: AI pair programmer free via GitHub Education.
tools.about:
AI pair programmer free via GitHub Education.

vs Codeium / Tabnine free tiers: Copilot has deeper context awareness (whole-repo indexing on Pro) and tighter VS Code/JetBrains integration. Free alternatives are fine for occasional use, but Copilot's multi-file context wins when your project has 50+ files.

tools.name: GitHub Pro (Education)
use_if: You use GitHub heavily and want branch protection rules on private repos, advanced code review (required reviewers, CODEOWNERS), Actions minutes bump, and Packages storage — the stuff that matters once your projects have collaborators or CI pipelines.
tools.tagline: Pro features while student-verified — private extras beyond free plan.
tools.about:
Pro features while student-verified — private extras beyond free plan.

vs GitHub Free: Free gives you unlimited private repos and 2,000 Actions minutes, which is enough for solo work. Pro adds required reviewers, Pages from private repos, and 3,000 Actions minutes. Claim Pro if you collaborate on private repos or run CI-heavy workflows; skip if you're solo on public repos.

tools.name: GitHub Student Developer Pack
use_if: You do one admin task per semester and forget about it — this single verification cascades into Copilot, domains, cloud credits, and dozens of tools without separate applications. Claim it on day one; everything else in this list gets easier after.
tools.tagline: One verification unlocks 80+ partner offers + Pro/Copilot/Codespaces.
tools.about:
One verification unlocks 80+ partner offers + Pro/Copilot/Codespaces.

vs applying to each vendor individually: one GitHub verification unlocks the majority of Pack-tagged entries below in minutes, while applying separately means repeating SheerID / .edu email flows per service and missing offers you didn't know existed.

program.needs: School email or proof of enrollment

tools.name: JetBrains All Products
use_if: You write Java, Kotlin, C#, or Python professionally-sized projects and need refactoring, debugging, and database tooling that actually understands your framework — not just syntax highlighting. The student license gives you _every_ IDE simultaneously, so you never hit a "wrong language" wall.
tools.tagline: IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm, Rider, CLion — full pack.
tools.about:
IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm, Rider, CLion — full pack.

vs VS Code + extensions: VS Code is lighter and free forever, but JetBrains wins on deep refactors, integrated profilers, and framework-aware inspections (Spring, Django, .NET). Pick JetBrains when the project is large enough that "go to definition" isn't enough.

tools.name: LocalStack (Pack)
use_if: You're learning AWS (Lambda, S3, DynamoDB, SQS, API Gateway) and want to iterate locally without worrying about credits or accidentally leaving resources running. The Pro license adds persistence, IAM enforcement, and advanced services that the free Community edition lacks.
tools.tagline: Full AWS emulator — practice without burning credits.
tools.about:
Full AWS emulator — practice without burning credits.

vs AWS Free Tier / real AWS sandbox: Real AWS teaches you billing and IAM reality but punishes mistakes with charges. LocalStack lets you `terraform apply` fearlessly and run integration tests offline. Use LocalStack for fast dev loops; validate on real AWS only before deploy.

tools.name: MATLAB Campus-Wide / Online
catches: Only if your school pays for it
use_if: Your coursework requires Simulink, Signal Processing, or Control Systems toolboxes that cost thousands commercially — the campus license bundles them all at zero cost. Also essential if professors hand out `.m` homework files with no alternative accepted.
tools.tagline: Full toolbox suite + browser MATLAB if your uni licenses it.
tools.about:
Full toolbox suite + browser MATLAB if your uni licenses it.

vs Python (NumPy/SciPy) / GNU Octave: Python is free forever and more employable in industry, but won't run Simulink models or satisfy professors who grade `.m` files. Octave is syntax-compatible for basics but lacks toolboxes. Use MATLAB when the curriculum demands it; learn Python in parallel for career portability.

tools.name: Name.com (Pack)
use_if: You want a `.live` TLD for a hackathon demo, project showcase, or streaming brand — it's instant via Pack and gives you a real custom domain to point at Vercel/Cloudflare Pages/your VPS for a year.
tools.tagline: Free domain year via GitHub Pack — alternate to Namecheap .me.
tools.about:
Free domain year via GitHub Pack — alternate to Namecheap .me.

vs Namecheap .me (also Pack) / buying a .dev or .com: Namecheap gives `.me` which is better for personal portfolio branding ("yourname.me"). Name.com `.live` is quirkier — good for event sites or streaming. If you want a serious long-term domain (.com/.dev), buy one for $10-12/yr and use these freebies for experiments.

tools.name: Namecheap .me (Pack)
use_if: You want `yourname.me` pointing at your portfolio site today — zero cost for 12 months with SSL included. A custom domain makes Vercel/Netlify/GitHub Pages deploys look professional instead of living on a `.vercel.app` subdomain.

skip_if.reason: Cloudflare Registrar: Cloudflare sells domains at cost with free DNS/proxy, but doesn't offer a free year. Namecheap's Pack deal gives you the first year free — grab it now, then transfer to Cloudflare at renewal if you want cheaper long-term pricing and built-in CDN.

tools.tagline: Free domain year for a portfolio.
tools.about: Free domain year for a portfolio.

tools.name: Notion Education
use_if: You organize everything — notes, project boards, reading lists, job applications — in one tool and want the Plus plan's unlimited blocks, file uploads, and AI features without paying $10/mo. School email verification is instant.
tools.tagline: Plus-class notes; Pack adds extra AI responses.
tools.about:
Plus-class notes; Pack adds extra AI responses.

vs Obsidian / Logseq (free, local-first): Obsidian is free forever with no vendor lock-in and works offline, but lacks real-time collaboration and requires plugin setup for databases/kanban. Notion wins if you collaborate on group projects or prefer structured databases; Obsidian wins if you want ownership of your `.md` files post-graduation.

tools.name: Perplexity Pro Student
use_if: You write research papers or need to quickly synthesize sources with proper citations — Perplexity Pro gives you unlimited Pro searches with source links, making it a turbo-charged literature review tool that actually shows where claims come from.
tools.tagline: Research AI with citations — often 1 year free.
tools.about:
Research AI with citations — often 1 year free.

vs ChatGPT Plus / Google Scholar: ChatGPT hallucinates citations; Perplexity's inline sources let you verify instantly. Google Scholar is authoritative but requires you to read and synthesize manually. Perplexity sits between them — AI speed with citation accountability.

perks: Research AI with citations — often 1 year free.

tools.name: Simple Analytics (Pack)
use_if: You have a portfolio site, blog, or side project and want to know what pages get traffic without selling your visitors' data to Google — Simple Analytics is GDPR-compliant by default, needs no cookie banner, and the dashboard is refreshingly simple.
tools.tagline: Privacy-first analytics — Starter free for a year via Pack.
tools.about:
Privacy-first analytics — Starter free for a year via Pack.

vs Google Analytics / Plausible / Umami: Google Analytics is free forever but requires cookie consent banners and sends visitor data to Google. Plausible is privacy-first but $9/mo with no student deal. Umami is self-hosted and free but needs your own server. Simple Analytics via Pack gives you hosted privacy analytics at zero cost for a year — the easiest ethical choice while you're a student.

perks: Privacy-first analytics — Starter free for a year via Pack.

tools.name: Stripe (Pack fee waiver)
use_if: You're building a real SaaS, marketplace, or side business that will process payments — the fee waiver on your first ~$1k in transactions means your early revenue isn't eaten by 2.9% + 30¢ per charge while you're validating product-market fit.
tools.tagline: Processing fee waiver on early volume via GitHub Student Pack.
tools.about:
Processing fee waiver on early volume via GitHub Student Pack.

vs starting without the waiver / Lemon Squeezy / Paddle: Without the waiver you lose ~$30 per $1k processed — small but meaningful at student scale. Lemon Squeezy and Paddle are merchant-of-record (simpler tax handling) but take 5-8% cuts with no student discount. Stripe + this waiver is the cheapest path for early direct payment processing.

tools.name: Termius Premium (Pack)
use_if: You SSH into servers from multiple devices (laptop, phone, tablet) and want your hosts, keys, and snippets synced everywhere with a polished UI — especially useful when managing cloud VMs, lab machines, or homelab boxes from anywhere.
tools.tagline: SSH synced across laptop and phone.
tools.about:
SSH synced across laptop and phone.

vs native SSH + config file / Blink (iOS): A plain `~/.ssh/config` is free and works great on one machine, but doesn't sync to mobile or handle SFTP visually. Blink is iOS-only and pricey post-student. Termius wins on cross-platform sync and team snippet sharing while the Pack license lasts.

tools.name: Unity Student
use_if: You're building games or interactive 3D experiences and want the Pro runtime features (dark theme aside — splash screen removal, runtime profiling, and priority bug fixes) without the $2k/yr price tag. Essential for game dev courses and portfolio pieces.
tools.tagline: Unity Pro Editor for verified students 16+.
tools.about:
Unity Pro Editor for verified students 16+.

vs Godot / Unreal Engine: Godot is fully free and open-source but has a smaller asset ecosystem and weaker console export. Unreal is free until $1M revenue but demands beefy hardware and C++ comfort. Unity Student hits the sweet spot for 2D/mobile/VR prototyping on modest hardware with the largest tutorial ecosystem.

tools.name: Working Copy (Pack)
use_if: You code or review PRs from an iPad/iPhone and want full Git operations (clone, branch, push, conflict resolution) with a native iOS UI — especially useful for iPad-as-laptop workflows with Shortcuts and Files integration.
tools.tagline: iOS Git client Pro unlocked via GitHub Student Pack.
tools.about:
iOS Git client Pro unlocked via GitHub Student Pack.

vs GitHub Mobile / web editor: GitHub Mobile lets you review and merge PRs but can't do local branching, rebasing, or work offline. The web editor is limited to single-file edits. Working Copy is a real Git client — pick it if you genuinely develop on iOS, skip it if your iPad is just for reading.

tools.name: Zyte Scrapy Cloud (Pack)
use_if: You have Scrapy spiders and want them running on a schedule in the cloud without maintaining a server or Docker cron. The Pack gives you one persistent unit — enough for a personal data pipeline that scrapes daily.

skip_if.reason: self-hosted Scrapy + cron: Zyte handles scheduling, log storage (120 days), and scaling without you babysitting a VPS. The tradeoff is vendor lock-in to their platform.
Apify free tier: Apify is broader (Puppeteer, Playwright, any scraper); Zyte is Scrapy-native. If your spiders are already Scrapy, Zyte deploys them as-is with zero rewrite.

tools.tagline: One Scrapy Cloud unit forever via Pack.
tools.about: One Scrapy Cloud unit forever via Pack.

tools.name: AWS Educate
use_if: You want to learn AWS services (Lambda, S3, DynamoDB, EC2) hands-on in sandboxed labs without risking a surprise bill. The badges look good on LinkedIn and the labs teach real console workflows — but you can't deploy your own production app here.

skip_if.reason: DigitalOcean/Heroku credits: Those give you real hosting for real projects. AWS Educate is a classroom — you learn the AWS way, but you don't get a public URL you can put in a portfolio. Use Educate for learning, DO/Heroku for shipping.

tools.tagline: Learning paths, badges, sandboxed labs.
tools.about: Learning paths, badges, sandboxed labs.

tools.name: DigitalOcean (Pack)
use_if: You want real Linux VMs (droplets) you fully control — SSH in, install anything, run Docker — or a simple App Platform deploy with zero Kubernetes overhead. Best bang-per-credit for hosting side projects that need a static IP and root access.

skip_if.reason: Heroku gives you push-to-deploy simplicity but zero SSH and no raw VM. DigitalOcean gives you the whole machine. Pick DO when you need custom Nginx configs, background workers, or GPU experimentation; pick Heroku when you just want `git push` and done.

tools.tagline: Platform credit for droplets and App Platform.
tools.about: Platform credit for droplets and App Platform.

tools.name: Heroku (Pack)
use_if: You want the fastest path from `git push` to a live URL — no Dockerfiles, no infrastructure YAML, no SSH. The 24-month runway means your capstone demo stays online through graduation without babysitting.

skip_if.reason: DO gives you a whole VM to configure yourself. Heroku abstracts all of that away: add a Postgres add-on with one click, scale dynos with a slider. You trade control for speed — ideal when shipping matters more than learning ops.

tools.tagline: Simple PaaS credit for 24 months.
tools.about: Simple PaaS credit for 24 months.

tools.name: MongoDB Atlas Credits (Pack)
use_if: Your app speaks MongoDB (Mongoose, Motor, or the native driver) and you want a managed cluster with backups, search indexes, and Charts without paying until $50 runs out. The free University cert is a résumé line that actually signals competence.

skip_if.reason: Supabase/Neon free tiers: Those are relational (Postgres). Atlas wins if your data is document-shaped (nested JSON, variable schemas). If you need joins and strict types, use a relational free tier instead.

tools.tagline: Stacks on top of free M0 forever tier.
tools.about: Stacks on top of free M0 forever tier.

tools.name: Boot.dev (Pack)
use_if: You want a gamified, opinionated backend path (Go, Python, SQL, Docker, CI/CD) that feels like a game with XP and streaks — and you specifically want backend/infra skills, not frontend. The curriculum is tight and builds toward "deploy a real service" not "pass a quiz."

skip_if.reason: The Odin Project: Boot.dev is structured and gamified with a single language path; Odin is community-driven, broader (full-stack), and free forever but requires more self-direction.
freeCodeCamp: Boot.dev focuses on backend/systems (Go, algorithms, Linux); freeCodeCamp is frontend-heavy (HTML/CSS/JS/React) with backend as an afterthought.

tools.tagline: Backend / DevOps learning path.
tools.about: Backend / DevOps learning path.

tools.name: DataCamp (Pack)
limits: Other seats via vendor donate partners
use_if: You need structured ramp-up on pandas, SQL, ML basics, or stats — and you learn best by doing exercises in a notebook-style environment rather than watching lectures. Great as a supplement alongside a CS degree, not a replacement.

skip_if.reason: Kaggle Learn: DataCamp has longer guided paths and career tracks; Kaggle Learn is micro-courses (2–4 hrs) best for quick refreshers. DataCamp wins on breadth, Kaggle on speed.
Coursera ML Specialization: Andrew Ng goes deeper on theory; DataCamp gets you writing sklearn/pandas code faster with less math preamble.

tools.tagline: Data and ML course supplement.
tools.about: Data and ML course supplement.

perks: Other seats via vendor donate partners

tools.name: Educative (Pack)
use_if: You're grinding system design or coding interviews and prefer reading + in-browser coding over watching videos. The "Grokking" series lives here and it's genuinely the fastest path to FAANG-style system design fluency.

skip_if.reason: LeetCode Premium: Educative teaches patterns and mental models; LeetCode is pure drill. Use both — Educative first to learn the framework, then LeetCode to build speed.
AlgoExpert: Educative has broader coverage (system design, ML, cloud) and text-first format vs AlgoExpert's video-heavy approach.

tools.tagline: Interactive courses — system design, interviews.
tools.about: Interactive courses — system design, interviews.

tools.name: Frontend Masters (Pack)
use_if: You want to mass-level frontend skills (React, TypeScript, performance) or go deep on systems (Rust, compilers, networking) with video courses taught by actual library authors — not random YouTubers.

skip_if.reason: Udemy/Coursera: FM is curated and opinionated — 200 courses from working engineers, not 200k courses of variable quality. No certificates, but real skill.
Pluralsight: FM's instructors ship frameworks you actually use (Webpack, Vite, Svelte). Pluralsight skews enterprise/.NET.

tools.tagline: Deep frontend and systems courses.
tools.about: Deep frontend and systems courses.

tools.name: AWS Activate
use_if: Your production infra is already on AWS (or will be) and you need runway to defer cloud bills for 12–24 months. The credits burn on anything — EC2, RDS, Bedrock — so they're most valuable when you'd otherwise be paying cash for compute-heavy workloads. vs Google for Startups: AWS credits cover more SKUs but require an accelerator/partner voucher for the big packages; GCP gives similar amounts with a simpler solo-founder application. vs Azure: AWS ecosystem is deeper for startups shipping containers + managed Postgres; Azure wins if your stack is .NET or you want bundled OpenAI credits.
tools.tagline: Startup cloud credits — apply via accelerator/partner or Activate Founders.
tools.about: Startup cloud credits — apply via accelerator/partner or Activate Founders.

tools.name: Google for Startups Cloud
use_if: You're building on BigQuery, Vertex AI, or Cloud Run and want $2k–$200k in credits without needing an accelerator sponsor. Google's application is friendlier to solo founders and pre-revenue teams than AWS Activate's partner path. vs AWS Activate: easier solo application, but GCP's managed-service catalog is thinner outside data/ML; if you're mostly running containers + Postgres, AWS has more battle-tested defaults. vs Azure: GCP wins for data pipelines and ML-native workloads; Azure wins for enterprise identity (Entra ID) and OpenAI API access bundled in.
tools.tagline: GCP credits for eligible startups — pair with Skills Boost for learning.
tools.about: GCP credits for eligible startups — pair with Skills Boost for learning.

tools.name: Microsoft for Startups
use_if: Your product depends on OpenAI models (GPT-4, embeddings) or your customers live in Microsoft-land (Teams integrations, Entra ID SSO). The bundled GitHub Enterprise + Azure OpenAI access is uniquely valuable for AI-first startups that need production-grade rate limits day one. vs AWS Activate: Azure credits are smaller on average but the OpenAI + GitHub bundle is unmatched; AWS wins on raw infra breadth and community tooling. vs Google for Startups: pick Azure when you need GPT-family models or .NET hosting; pick GCP when your differentiator is data/ML pipelines on Vertex.
